prompt: Build a small card for a support team's weekly review that shows tickets opened versus tickets resolved for the last 12 weeks. Opened: 120, 135, 128, 150, 162, 158, 171, 166, 180, 175, 169, 160. Resolved: 110, 125, 130, 140, 150, 155, 160, 168, 170, 172, 171, 168. The team lead wants to know whether the backlog is shrinking. Draw the chart as inline SVG inside a single self-contained HTML file with no external assets, and make sure the whole card is visible without scrolling.
rubric: Both series are drawn as lines (or another honest form for change over time) and the card is clearly about opened versus resolved tickets.
Each series is named by a label at or beside its line rather than only by a legend far from the data.
The value axis is labeled with a unit and its baseline is honest; gridlines, if any, are faint, with no 3D, shadows or gradients.
The answer to the lead's question (the gap is closing, resolved has caught up with opened) is stated in the title or an annotation.
The two series are distinguishable without relying on red versus green or hue alone.

prompt: Show the results of a product survey question, 'Which features do you use?', in a single self-contained HTML file with no external assets. 420 people answered and each could pick several features. Results: Search 71%, Tags 48%, Sharing 35%, Export 22%, Templates 15%. It goes in a product update newsletter, so keep it tidy and readable at a glance.
rubric: Uses bars (or dots) rather than a pie or donut, since the answers do not add up to 100%.
Features are sorted by value and each bar shows its percentage as a visible label.
States the base: 420 respondents and that several answers were allowed.
Uses one color or a muted palette with one emphasis rather than a different saturated hue per bar.
Bars start at zero on a scale that runs to 100% or to the largest value without distortion.

prompt: A teammate made this chart for a finance review and asked me to critique it: a 3D pie of eight expense categories (payroll, rent, software, travel, marketing, legal, supplies, other), each slice a different bright rainbow color, a legend along the bottom, and no percentages or values printed anywhere. What should change? Give a prioritized list.
rubric: Recommends replacing the pie with sorted bars, and says why (eight parts are hard to compare by angle).
Recommends putting values on the chart and labeling directly instead of using a bottom legend.
Recommends dropping the 3D effect and reducing the rainbow to one hue or gray with a highlight.
Suggests grouping tiny categories into 'Other' with a note about what it contains, or a similar way to cut clutter.
The list is prioritized and concrete rather than a generic design lecture.

prompt: We want one chart showing monthly revenue (in dollars) and order count, and our dashboard tool defaults to putting them on two y-axes. Should we do that? Answer in under 150 words.
rubric: Explains that two independent axes make crossings and apparent correlation arbitrary.
Offers at least one concrete alternative: two aligned charts, indexing both series, or a ratio such as revenue per order.
Gives a clear recommendation rather than only listing considerations.
Stays under about 150 words.

rubric: The value axis starts at zero so bar lengths match the values.
The gradient fills are replaced with flat solid color.
Category names are readable without rotation (for example horizontal bars or shorter labels).
The legend for a single series is removed and replaced by a title or axis label that gives the unit.
Values are labeled on the bars or gridlines are kept faint; the chart stays visually quiet.

prompt: Our 20-year chart of average rent in dollars shows a steep rise, and a reviewer says it is misleading. Explain what they probably mean and what to do. Under 150 words.
rubric: Explains that nominal dollars mix price-level change with real change.
Suggests inflation-adjusted values, an index, or rent as a share of income, naming the base year or base period.
May suggest showing both nominal and adjusted lines.
Stays under about 150 words.

prompt: Plan a figure for a quarterly business review comparing monthly sales of nine product lines over three years. Describe the layout, scales, ordering, labeling and what to highlight. Keep it to a short plan.
rubric: Proposes small multiples (one small chart per product line) rather than nine lines in one plot.
Uses a shared scale for comparison, or explicitly justifies independent scales with a visible note.
Orders the panels by something meaningful (such as total sales or growth) instead of defaulting to alphabetical.
Includes a reference such as an average line or highlights the lines that matter.
Describes compact labeling: panel names, scale shown once per row or column.

prompt: For a nonprofit's one-page annual report, show how each donated dollar was spent: programs 78%, fundraising 12%, administration 10%. Keep it friendly. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with no external assets.
rubric: A clear part-to-whole graphic (pie, donut, 100% bar or similar) is used and any of these forms is acceptable here.
All three parts show their values on or beside the graphic.
There is no 3D, shadow or gradient effect, and the parts add up to 100%.
The tone is friendly and readable in the first screen without clutter.

prompt: Design a header strip for an analytics page that shows three key numbers for this month: active users 18,420 (last month 17,150), revenue $92,300 (last month $96,800), and churn 2.4% (last month 2.9%). Each should be compared with last month. One self-contained HTML file with no external assets.
rubric: The three numbers are the most prominent elements, each with its comparison to last month.
Direction and size of the change are conveyed in text or a symbol, not by color alone.
No full-size charts are added to what is a strip of key numbers; any trend lines stay small and secondary.
Number formatting is consistent and the churn change is not mislabeled (a fall in churn is an improvement).

prompt: Write a short guide to formatting a spreadsheet column of currency values so it prints cleanly.
rubric: Covers alignment of the numbers, a consistent number of decimal places, and where the currency symbol goes.
Covers how to show negative values.
Does not push the reader to convert the column into a chart.
Is concise and practical.
